name: logos
workload: Criterion micro-benchmarks tokenizing identifiers, keywords/operators/punctuators, and quoted strings; throughput reported in MB/s
claimed_speedup: README states its explicit goal is 'to make the generated Lexer faster than anything you'd write by hand'; benchmark throughput: identifiers 1204 MB/s (647 ns/iter), keywords/operators/punctuators 1037 MB/s (2054 ns/iter), strings 1575 MB/s (553 ns/iter) -- no paired number against a specific hand-written lexer is shown
tradeoffs: Requires derive-macro codegen at compile time; combines all tokens into one DFA with lookup/jump tables and unrolled loops; Rust only, less flexible for irregular/ambiguous grammars than a bespoke hand lexer
caveats: The 'faster than hand-written' claim is a design goal stated in prose, not a paired benchmark number against a named hand-written lexer; no CPU model or rustc version is given for the throughput numbers, so this is capped at tier C
found_via: Blogs/talks: WebSearch query 'rust logos crate faster than hand-written lexer benchmark' surfaced logos's own README claim, which is also cited as the bar to beat by other lexer blog posts found in this search

name: simd-lexing
workload: Lexing a single concatenated file of all GCC source code (identifiers/strings/comments; does not parse numeric literals) on a Skylake 2.40GHz i5 laptop
claimed_speedup: flex 231ms, flex --fast 102ms, flex --full 106ms, simd-lex 34ms => roughly 6.8x faster than plain flex and ~3x faster than flex --fast/--full (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Single-header, table-free AVX2 lexer customized via macros; author describes it as 'more of a proof-of-concept'; limited to a fixed set of token classes, no code generation from a grammar
caveats: First-party README numbers only; compiler and build flags used for the flex vs simd-lex comparison are not stated, and it is unclear if flex's output was itself compiled with optimization flags matching simd-lex's
found_via: Blogs/talks: WebSearch query 'fast SIMD lexer tokenizer blog benchmark vs re2c hand-written' surfaced this project via a discussion referencing SIMD lexing approaches (Parabix/simdjson lineage)

name: lexer-exp (SIMD NEON lexer experiments, dist1ll)
baseline: hand-written lexer (author's naive baseline) and the logos lexer-generator crate
workload: Tokenizing ~100KB of synthetic pseudocode (~8k lines) and, in a follow-up, real-world source snippets from Oxide's Hubris kernel (5KB-1MB files), using a hand-rolled SIMD lexer built with ARMv8 NEON intrinsics and perfect-hash keyword matching
claimed_speedup: ~2x faster than the author's original naive hand-written lexer on Apple M1 (174,476 ns/iter vs 312,837 ns/iter); ~35% faster than logos on the synthetic pseudocode benchmark; but ~18% SLOWER than logos on realistic Hubris kernel data (89,151 ns/iter vs 108,257 ns/iter); author summarizes an overall 20-30% speedup vs logos across realistic 5KB-1MB files
compiler_and_flags: Rust, --release profile, with #[inline(always)] and #[no_mangle] on hot functions; exact rustc version not stated
hardware: Apple M1 for the headline numbers; also tested on unspecified x86_64 hardware
tradeoffs: ARM NEON-specific code path (author notes x86_64 needs separate treatment); result is workload-dependent, sometimes losing to logos on realistic (non-repetitive) source; experimental research code from a personal compiler project, not a packaged library
caveats: Results are explicitly mixed by the author's own admission: SIMD lexer beats logos on synthetic pseudocode but loses on realistic kernel source; rustc version and the x86_64 CPU model are not given, so despite public benchmark code this is capped at tier C rather than A
found_via: Blogs/talks: WebSearch query 'fast SIMD lexer tokenizer blog benchmark vs re2c hand-written' surfaced the blog post 'Beating the fastest lexer generator in Rust' at alic.dev/blog/fast-lexing

name: Accelerated-Zig-Parser (compacting SIMD tokenizer)
baseline: Zig standard library tokenizer (hand-written, used by the Zig 0.14 self-hosted compiler)
workload: Tokenizing the Zig compiler's own source corpus (3,253 files, 3,504,899,722 lines, ~47GB) by processing 64-byte SIMD chunks at a time ('compacting' tokenizer)
claimed_speedup: 2.75x faster: 1.41 GB/s (compacting tokenizer) vs 0.51 GB/s (legacy std tokenizer); equivalently 105.25B lines-of-code/s vs 38.34B loc/s
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (requires AVX-512 support)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 (x86-64-v4) hardware to hit the headline numbers; tokenizer-focused (full parser is a separate, still-evolving component of the repo); a future 512-byte-chunk version is only planned, not yet benchmarked
caveats: Benchmark corpus and harness are the author's own (self-reported, single-run figures on the author's machine), not an independent or peer-reviewed suite; the blog post text is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 but that license applies to the writeup, not the MIT/Apache-2.0-licensed code
found_via: Blogs/talks: WebSearch query 'Zig tokenizer faster than hand-written lexer benchmark blog' surfaced Validark's blog post 'Deus Lex Machina'

name: Gigatoken
workload: Encoding the openwebtext corpus (owt_train.txt, 11.9GB) with BPE tokenizers for ~23 model families (GPT-2, Llama 3/3.1/3.2/3.3/4, Qwen 2/2.5/3/3.5/3.6, DeepSeek V3/R1/V4, GLM 4/5, Phi-4, Gemma, Mistral, etc.); Gigatoken tokenizes the whole file unsplit while HF tokenizers gets the first 100MB and tiktoken the first 1GB, both pre-split on the document separator
claimed_speedup: GPT-2 on AMD EPYC 9565 dual-socket (144 cores): 24.53 GB/s vs HF tokenizers' 24.8 MB/s (989x) and tiktoken's 36.0 MB/s (681x); other tokenizer families range roughly 9x-1300x depending on model and CPU (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D tables also given); SentencePiece-based tokenizers (Gemma, Mistral, CodeLlama) show the smallest gains, ~7-22x
hardware: AMD EPYC 9565 72-core x2 sockets (144 cores); Apple M4 Max (16 cores); AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D (16 cores)
tradeoffs: Its own native API is fastest; a compatibility-mode wrapper that guarantees byte-identical output to HuggingFace/tiktoken is noticeably slower than native mode; SentencePiece-family tokenizers are not well optimized yet; ships as a Python package (PyO3) backed by a Rust core
caveats: Benchmark setup gives Gigatoken the harder task (it must find its own split boundaries and parallelize the whole file) while HF/tiktoken are handed pre-split chunks, which the README argues is fair but is asymmetric; exact rustc version and build flags are not stated; this is the project's own first-party benchmark (amplified by AI-news blogs such as MarkTechPost) rather than an independent suite, so it is capped at tier C
found_via: Blogs/talks: WebSearch query 'conference talk fast tokenizer SIMD parsing CppCon RustConf benchmark' surfaced MarkTechPost/aggregator coverage of Gigatoken; numbers verified directly against the project's own README benchmark tables
